proposal.title: Tenancy for every kind of workspace: one owner record, workspace-neutral roles, invitations, a table per kind
proposal.summary: `tenant` becomes the parent of every kind of workspace and holds only what all kinds share; what one kind alone has lives in a one-to-one table keyed by `tenant_id` (`team` today, `gym` next), so a new kind is a new table and a lookup row, never a column on `tenant`. Ownership is recorded once, as the single `tenant_member` row with `role = 'owner'`. Roles mean the same thing in every kind of workspace, and which kind allows which role is data (`tenant_role`) enforced by composite foreign keys. An invitation to somebody with no account yet is its own table, so a membership row always names a real person. The gym PRD's standalone `gym`, `gym_branch` and `gym_staff` are superseded by `gym`, `gym_branch` and `tenant_member` as drawn here.

alter.description: A workspace: the unit of isolation. Every kind of workspace — solo, team, gym — is a row here, and this table holds only what all of them share; what is particular to one kind lives in a table of its own keyed by `tenant_id` (`team`, `gym`), so a new kind is a new table and a `tenant_role` row, never a column here. Who owns it is the one `tenant_member` row with `role = 'owner'`; who pays is `subscription`, keyed by trainer.

changeColumn.name: type
changeColumn.description: What kind of workspace. Fixed at creation — `freeze_tenant_type()` refuses any change, because a solo workspace that became a gym would take every row in it along. Paired with `id` in `uq_tenant_id_type` so the per-kind tables and `tenant_member` can carry a composite foreign key that proves the kind.

changeColumn.name: name
changeColumn.description: Shown in the workspace switcher. A solo workspace is created as its trainer's name, or 'My practice' when the trainer has no name yet or only their phone number, and follows the trainer's name (`follow_solo_tenant_name()`) until the owner names it something else.

changeColumn.name: status
changeColumn.description: Switches a whole workspace off with one column. `closed` is how a workspace ends: there is no `deleted_at`, because `tenant` never enters sync and so needs no tombstone.

addColumn.name: status_changed_at
addColumn.description: When `status` last moved, set by `set_tenant_status_changed_at()`. A suspension has to be datable for a support conversation and a closure for retention.

changeColumn.name: metadata
changeColumn.description: Free-form notes that nothing branches on. Anything the product reads is a typed column here or on the kind's own table. The creating triggers write nothing here.

dropColumn.name: primary_app_user_id
dropColumn.reason: A second record of the owner beside the `tenant_member` owner row (and a third beside `team.owner_trainer_id`), with nothing keeping them equal — and NULL for every signup, because the trainer row is saved before the `app_user` row, so `app_owns_tenant()` told the owner they did not own their own workspace. Ownership is the owner row; who pays is `subscription`.

dropColumn.name: deleted_at
dropColumn.reason: A second way to end a workspace beside `status = 'closed'`. `tenant` never enters sync, so it needs no tombstone.

dropIndex.name: idx_tenant_type
dropIndex.reason: Three values, and no query filters on the kind alone.

addIndex.name: uq_tenant_id_type
addIndex.description: The target of the composite foreign keys (`tenant_member`, `tenant_invite`, `team`, `gym`) that prove which kind of workspace a row belongs to.

createTable.name: tenant_role
createTable.description: Which roles exist in which kind of workspace — reference rows, written by the migration. Adding a role is an INSERT here rather than a DROP / ADD CONSTRAINT on a live table, and the composite key from `tenant_member` makes a `staff` member of a solo workspace impossible rather than merely unwritten. Not policied: it is the same for every caller, and the request role holds SELECT only.

column.name: tenant_type
column.description: A `tenant.type`.

column.name: role
column.description: A role that kind of workspace allows. The meanings are on `tenant_member.role`.

alter.description: Who is in a workspace, and as what — people only; an invitation to somebody who may have no account yet is `tenant_invite`. One row per person per role: a trainer who coaches privately and at a gym has two, and an owner who also coaches has two in one workspace. That row is for good — leaving marks it `removed`, and rejoining sets the same row back to `active` rather than writing a second, so `uq_tenant_member_live` needs no status in it. Only the current stint is kept (decided 24 Sep 2026: a gym does not ask who was on its staff on a past date); the dated `tenant_member_terms` rows are the one trace of an earlier one. The owner row is the only record of who owns a workspace. Team membership is mirrored in from `team_member` by trigger.

addColumn.name: tenant_type
addColumn.description: Copied from `tenant.type` on insert by `stamp_tenant_type()`. It exists so the two composite foreign keys can prove the role is one this kind of workspace has; it can never disagree with the tenant, because the first of them points at `tenant (id, type)`.

changeColumn.name: role
changeColumn.description: The same word means the same authority in every kind of workspace. `owner` — exactly one per workspace and cannot be removed; `admin` — manages people and plans; `coach` — holds a roster; `staff` — a gym's front desk or accountant, with no roster; `client` — reserved for the portal. Whether somebody coaches is whether they hold clients, not which role they have: an owner or admin may coach too. Which roles each kind of workspace allows is `tenant_role`.

changeColumn.name: status
changeColumn.description: A membership row always names a person who said yes; an invitation still waiting, or turned down, is a `tenant_invite`. Leaving or being removed sets `removed`; accepting a later invitation sets the same row back to `active` (`respond_tenant_invite()`).

addColumn.name: invited_by_member_id
addColumn.description: Who brought them in this time — the inviter's own membership row, copied from `tenant_invite` on accepting; a rejoin overwrites it with the new inviter. A membership and not an `app_user`, so the inviter provably belongs to this workspace: `tenant_member_invited_by_fkey` looks the row up by `(id, tenant_id)` with this row's `tenant_id`, and one from another workspace is not found. It also records the role they invited in. NULL on the owner row the signup triggers write, which nobody invited — a composite key with a NULL in it is not checked. It proves the inviter was a member here, not that they still are or were allowed to invite; that is checked when the invitation is written (`tenant_invite_staff`).

addColumn.name: joined_at
addColumn.description: When the current stint began. A rejoin resets it to the moment of accepting, so it never spans a gap in which they were not a member.

addColumn.name: ended_at
addColumn.description: When they last left or were removed. Set together with `status = 'removed'` and cleared by a rejoin; `tenant_member_ended` keeps the two in step.

changeColumn.name: is_home
changeColumn.description: The workspace the app opens in. Exactly one per person, and never a membership that has ended (`tenant_member_home_live`): leaving your home workspace moves `is_home` to another live membership in the same transaction.

dropColumn.name: revenue_share_percent
dropColumn.reason: A percentage edited in place: `TenantRevenueService` applies today's value to every past payment, so changing a coach's share from 60% to 70% rewrites last quarter. Moves to `tenant_member_terms`, which is dated.

dropColumn.name: assignment_margin_percent
dropColumn.reason: The same problem as `revenue_share_percent`; moves to `tenant_member_terms`.

dropForeignKey.name: tenant_member_tenant_id_fkey
dropForeignKey.reason: Replaced by `tenant_member_tenant_kind_fkey`, which checks the kind as well.

addIndex.name: uq_tenant_member_id_tenant
addIndex.description: The target of the composite foreign keys that prove a membership is in the same workspace as the row pointing at it: `tenant_member.invited_by_member_id`, and `tenant_invite.invited_by_member_id` and `.member_id`. Redundant as uniqueness, since `id` alone is unique; it exists only so a foreign key can name the pair.

dropCheck.name: tenant_member_role
dropCheck.reason: `tenant_role` replaces it, per kind of workspace.

dropCheck.name: tenant_member_status
dropCheck.reason: Replaced by the narrower list below.

addIndex.name: uq_tenant_member_owner
addIndex.description: One owner per workspace. This row is the only record of ownership, so it has to be exactly one.

addTrigger.name: trg_tenant_member_stamp_type
addTrigger.description: Fires after `trg_tenant_member_stamp_tenant` (same timing, so name order), which has already filled `tenant_id`.

createTable.name: tenant_invite
createTable.description: An invitation to join a workspace, addressed to a phone that may have no account yet — which is why it is not a `tenant_member` row, whose `app_user_id` is NOT NULL. Every kind of workspace invites through this one table. Claimed by signing in on that phone and calling `respond_tenant_invite()`, which writes the `tenant_member` row; expiry is read from `expires_at` and never stored as a status. Nobody is invited as `owner` — ownership is transferred, not offered.

column.name: tenant_id
column.description: The workspace they are invited into.

column.name: tenant_type
column.description: Copied from `tenant.type` by `stamp_tenant_type()`, for the same two composite keys as `tenant_member`.

column.name: phone
column.description: Who it is for, in the same shape as `app_user.phone`. The invitation is theirs to read once they sign in on it.

column.name: role
column.description: The role they will hold on accepting. Any role the kind of workspace allows except `owner`.

column.name: invited_by_member_id
column.description: Who sent it: the sender's own membership row in this workspace, copied onto the membership on accepting. `tenant_invite_invited_by_fkey` looks it up by `(id, tenant_id)`, so a member of another workspace cannot be named as the sender. That it is the caller's own row, still `active`, and `owner` or `admin` is checked by `tenant_invite_staff` on insert — a constraint would also reject history rows once the sender later leaves.

column.name: expires_at
column.description: A pending invitation past this is expired. Derived, never stored, so nothing has to sweep it.

column.name: responded_at
column.description: When it left `pending`, whichever way.

column.name: member_id
column.description: The membership accepting it created — or reactivated: a rejoin's invitation points at the same row as the first one did. Keyed on `(member_id, tenant_id)` like the sender, so it can only be a membership in this workspace.

index.name: uq_tenant_invite_pending
index.description: One open invitation per person per role per workspace; resending refreshes it rather than stacking a second.

index.name: idx_tenant_invite_phone
index.description: What the invitee's sign-in asks: is anything waiting for this number?

createTable.name: tenant_member_terms
createTable.description: The commercial terms of one membership, dated. Replaces the two percentages that sat on `tenant_member`, where an edit silently rewrote every past period `TenantRevenueService` computes. Revenue for a payment uses the row in force on the payment's date. Append-only: a change closes the open row and writes another in the same transaction, so there is at most one open row per member. Terms end with the stint: leaving closes the open row on the day they leave, so a rejoin — which reuses the `tenant_member` row — starts with no terms in force and never inherits the earlier stint's share. Money tier: the active workspace only, and owners and admins only in code.

column.name: tenant_member_id
column.description: The membership these terms belong to.

column.name: revenue_share_percent
column.description: What this member keeps of what they collect in this workspace. NULL = 100%, the right answer for a solo workspace.

column.name: assignment_margin_percent
column.description: An admin's cut of revenue from clients they placed with somebody else. NULL = none. Still frozen per handover onto `client_assignment.actor_margin_percent`.

column.name: effective_from
column.description: The first day these terms apply.

column.name: effective_to
column.description: The first day they no longer apply. NULL on the terms in force now.

column.name: set_by_app_user_id
column.description: Who agreed them — a coach's pay is the one number on this table somebody will ask about.

checks.check: (revenue_share_percent IS NULL OR revenue_share_percent BETWEEN 0 AND 100) AND (assignment_margin_percent IS NULL OR assignment_margin_percent BETWEEN 0 AND 100)
effective_to IS NULL OR effective_to > effective_from

index.name: uq_tenant_member_terms_open
index.description: At most one set of terms in force per member.

index.name: idx_tenant_member_terms_member
index.description: The revenue read: which terms were in force on a payment's date.

changeColumn.name: owner_trainer_id
changeColumn.description: Still a second record of the owner, kept while `team_member` is separate. It goes when `team_member` folds into `tenant_member` + `tenant_invite` — a later pass, since teams are out of v1. Until then `ensure_team_tenant()` writes the owner's `tenant_member` row from it.

addColumn.name: tenant_type
addColumn.description: Always `team`. Exists for the composite key that proves this is a team workspace.

addIndex.name: uq_team_tenant
addIndex.description: One team per team workspace. Nothing enforced it, so two `team` rows could share one tenant.

createTable.name: gym
createTable.description: What only a gym has, one row per gym workspace, keyed by its `tenant_id`. Supersedes the gym PRD's standalone `gym` table, whose `owner_app_user_id` would have been another record of the owner, and its `gym_staff`, which is `tenant_member` with `role = 'admin'` or `'staff'`. The composite key to `tenant (id, type)` makes a gym row on a solo workspace impossible. Read by the workspace's members; written by its owner.

column.name: tenant_id
column.description: The gym's workspace — the gym is that tenant, not a separate thing it points at.

column.name: tenant_type
column.description: Always `gym`, for the composite key.

column.name: legal_name
column.description: The name on its invoices, when it differs from `tenant.name`.

column.name: gstin
column.description: Its GST number, for the invoices a gym client receives.

createTable.name: gym_branch
createTable.description: A gym's locations. There from the start for the reason the gym PRD gives: a branch added later is a nullable column on every gym-owned table and a back-fill that has to guess. Hangs off `gym`, so only a gym workspace can have one.

column.name: tenant_id
column.description: The gym it belongs to.

addTrigger.name: trg_trainer_follow_solo_name
addTrigger.description: A solo workspace's name follows the trainer's until the owner renames it.

function.name: app_user_id()
function.description: The caller's `app_user.id`, a seventh connection setting beside the six `TenantAwareDataSource` already sets. Ownership is a membership keyed by `app_user_id`, so the ownership test should match on that and not on a phone number, which `IDENTITY.md` shows can be recycled.

function.name: app_owns_tenant(uuid)
function.description: Reads the owner membership instead of `tenant.primary_app_user_id`. Stays VOLATILE for V21's reason (the team policy asks it about a tenant written earlier in the same statement), and stays revoked from PUBLIC.
function.sql: CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION public.app_owns_tenant(target uuid) RETURNS boolean LANGUAGE sql SECURITY DEFINER SET search_path TO 'public', 'pg_catalog' AS $$ SELECT EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM tenant_member tm JOIN tenant t ON t.id = tm.tenant_id WHERE tm.tenant_id = target AND tm.app_user_id = app_user_id() AND tm.role = 'owner' AND tm.status = 'active' AND tm.deleted_at IS NULL AND t.status <> 'closed' ); $$;

function.name: ensure_home_tenant()
function.description: No `primary_app_user_id`, no back-pointer in `metadata`, and a name that is the phone number is treated as no name. The owner row is still written by `ensure_home_membership` / `ensure_membership_for_user`, whichever of `trainer` and `app_user` is inserted second — which is what makes signup order stop mattering.

function.name: ensure_team_tenant()
function.description: Now also writes the owner's membership. The `team` policy's WITH CHECK asks `app_owns_tenant()` about the new tenant in this same statement, and ownership is now the membership row — which `mirror_team_member` would only write later, from `team_member`. Refuses a team whose owner has no account rather than creating an ownerless workspace.

function.name: mirror_team_member()
function.description: Mirrors only what is now a membership: an `active` team member becomes (or becomes again) an active `tenant_member`, a `removed` one ends it. `invited` and `declined` team rows stay out — an invitation is not a membership. Goes entirely when `team_member` folds into `tenant_member` + `tenant_invite`.

function.name: freeze_tenant_type()
set_tenant_status_changed_at()
stamp_tenant_type()
function.description: Fills `tenant_type` from the tenant when the writer left it out. SECURITY DEFINER so it can read a tenant the caller is not yet a member of (an invitation's accept path); a wrong value supplied by a writer is refused by the composite foreign key regardless.

function.name: follow_solo_tenant_name()
function.description: Renames a solo workspace with its trainer, but only while the workspace still carries the default or the trainer's previous name — once the owner has named it themselves, it is theirs.
function.sql:
CREATE FUNCTION public.follow_solo_tenant_name() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql SECURITY DEFINER SET search_path TO 'public', 'pg_catalog' AS $$ BEGIN UPDATE tenant t SET name = TRIM(NEW.name) WHERE t.id = NEW.home_tenant_id AND t.type = 'solo' AND NULLIF(TRIM(NEW.name), '') IS NOT NULL AND TRIM(NEW.name) <> NEW.phone AND t.name IN ('My practice', COALESCE(TRIM(OLD.name), '')); RETURN NULL; END $$;
CREATE TRIGGER trg_trainer_follow_solo_name AFTER UPDATE OF name ON public.trainer FOR EACH ROW WHEN (NEW.name IS DISTINCT FROM OLD.name) EXECUTE FUNCTION public.follow_solo_tenant_name();

function.name: respond_tenant_invite(uuid, boolean)
function.description: The invitee's only write. The request role cannot insert `tenant_member` (V21), so accepting has to be a definer function; it checks the caller is the invited person — by account id and by phone — and that the invitation is still open. Declining goes through the same door so the invitee needs no UPDATE policy of their own.

policies.policy: Not policied — reference rows, identical for every caller. `GRANT SELECT` to the request role and nothing else; joins the not-policied list in `SCHEMA.md` with that reason.

`tenant_invite_staff` — FOR ALL to staff: reads across `app_tenant_ids()`, writes only into `app_tenant_id()`, and its WITH CHECK requires `invited_by_member_id` to be one of the caller's own memberships there — `EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM tenant_member m WHERE m.id = invited_by_member_id AND m.app_user_id = app_user_id() AND m.status = 'active' AND m.role IN ('owner', 'admin') AND m.deleted_at IS NULL)` — so nobody can send an invitation in another member's name or after they have left. The foreign key already puts the sender in the same workspace; this puts the caller behind it. Who may invite is also checked in code, as for every other membership write. `tenant_invite_invitee` — FOR SELECT where `phone = app_phone()` and `app_phone() <> ''`, so an invitee can see what is waiting before they are a member of anything. Grants: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE; no DELETE (revoke by status).
Tier 2, the money tier: `tenant_id = app_tenant_id()` for staff, reads and writes. Grants: SELECT, INSERT, and UPDATE (closing `effective_to` only, enforced in code); no DELETE.

Read by members (`tenant_id = ANY (app_tenant_ids())`); UPDATE only when `app_owns_tenant(tenant_id)`. No INSERT policy: a gym workspace and its `gym` row are created together by a definer function, like the solo and team triggers.
Tier 1: staff read across `app_tenant_ids()` and write into `app_tenant_id()`; owner / admin gate in code. No DELETE — soft-deleted.
`tenant_self` (SELECT) and `tenant_owner_update` (UPDATE) are unchanged in text; `tenant_owner_update` now means "the owner membership" because `app_owns_tenant()` does.

code.item: Set a seventh setting, `app.user_id`, alongside the six it already sets in one round trip; `app_user_id()` reads it.
`GYM_ADMIN` / `GYM_STAFF` become `ADMIN` / `STAFF`; `ADMINISTERS` and `READS_TENANT_REVENUE` become `{OWNER, ADMIN}`.
`t.deleted_at IS NULL` becomes `t.status <> 'closed'`; the membership read takes the two percentages from the open `tenant_member_terms` row.

`updateEconomics` closes the open terms row and inserts a new one instead of updating `tenant_member`. The response keeps both percentage fields — the additive law — they are simply read from the terms.

Leaving and removing are one write: `status = 'removed'` and `ended_at = now()`, the open `tenant_member_terms` row closed on the same day, and `is_home` moved to another live membership when the ended one held it. A rejoin is never written here — it arrives through `respond_tenant_invite()`, which reactivates the row.
The share is the terms row in force on each payment's date, not today's.

New walls to assert: one owner per workspace; `staff` refused in a solo workspace; `tenant.type` refused a change; team creation still passes `team_tenant` with ownership moved; an invitation accepted from the wrong phone or account refused; an expired invitation refused; leaving then accepting a new invitation reuses the same `tenant_member` row with `joined_at` reset and no terms in force; accepting while still an active member refused; a removed row refused `is_home`; an invitation naming a sender's membership from another workspace refused by the foreign key; an invitation naming another member's row, a removed row, or a `coach` or `staff` row as the sender refused by `tenant_invite_staff`.

The gym PRD's `gym` / `gym_staff` replaced by this shape; `tenant_role`, `tenant_invite` and `tenant_member_terms` documented; the role list rewritten. Also worth noting there: the PRD's planned `client.gym_id` is the same fact as "this client's `tenant_id` is a gym workspace", so it may not need to exist — to be settled when the gym tables are reviewed.

proposal.title: Deleting an account is an erasure: the person's data goes, the ledgers keep only counts
proposal.summary: Decided 24 Sep 2026, to meet the DPDP Act's erasure duty. `DELETE /v1/trainers/me` (and, when the portal ships, a client's own account delete) stops being a soft delete and becomes `erase_account()`, one transaction: (1) the person's **solo workspace is closed** and emptied by the purge job; (2) they are **removed from every other workspace**; (3) a **team or gym they own blocks the delete** until they hand it on with `transfer_tenant_ownership()`. Support can instead pass `leave_owned`, which leaves that workspace with no owner until support assigns one. (4) **Every name, number and piece of free text** about them and about their solo workspace's clients is deleted or set to NULL, and so is every client row carrying their number on anybody's roster. (5) The `app_user`, `trainer` and `client` rows stay as **tombstones**: an id and dates, with the personal columns NULL, and a CHECK that makes an incomplete scrub unwritable. The phone number is **released**. What stays is audit without identity: `erasure_log` (what was erased, when, row counts), `subscription` (our billing), `privacy_accepted_at` (consent evidence), and, in workspaces the person did not own, sessions and payments as amounts and dates against a client or coach who has no name. Workspace delete — the other case — reuses `purge_after` / `purged_at` and is a later proposal.

changeColumn.name: phone
changeColumn.description: UNIQUE. The login. NULL only on an erased account (`app_user_erased`): erasure releases the number, and NULLs never collide in the unique index, so the next person to hold the SIM signs up as a stranger rather than landing on a tombstone. No hash is kept — a ten-digit number's hash is the number.

addColumn.name: erased_at
addColumn.description: When `erase_account()` removed this person. The row stays as a tombstone, so the ids in `tenant_member`, `tenant_invite`, `subscription` and `erasure_log` still resolve; `role` and `privacy_accepted_at` stay too — consent evidence names no one once the phone is gone. Distinct from `deleted_at`, which erasure also sets, so everything that already filters `deleted_at IS NULL` keeps working unchanged.

alter.addCheck: (erased_at IS NULL) = (phone IS NOT NULL) AND (erased_at IS NULL OR deleted_at IS NOT NULL)

changeColumn.name: phone
changeColumn.description: UNIQUE. NULL only on an erased trainer; released with `app_user.phone`.

changeColumn.name: name
changeColumn.description: NULL only on an erased trainer. A gym or team that keeps this coach's logged sessions draws them as a former coach.

addColumn.name: erased_at
addColumn.description: When the trainer was erased. The row stays so the `trainer_id` on sessions and payments in workspaces they did not own still resolves. `trainer_erased_scrubbed` lists every personal column, so a scrub that misses one fails instead of succeeding quietly. **A new personal column on this table must be added to that CHECK in the same migration.**

alter.addCheck: erased_at IS NULL AND phone IS NOT NULL AND name IS NOT NULL OR erased_at IS NOT NULL AND deleted_at IS NOT NULL AND phone IS NULL AND name IS NULL AND email IS NULL AND upi_vpa IS NULL AND fcm_token IS NULL AND headline IS NULL AND bio IS NULL AND intro_video_url IS NULL AND map_link IS NULL AND instagram_url IS NULL AND youtube_url IS NULL AND gym_name IS NULL AND gender IS NULL AND experience_band IS NULL AND specialities = '[]' AND certifications = '[]' AND languages = '[]' AND training_modes = '[]' AND service_areas = '[]' AND metadata = '{}'

changeColumn.name: name
changeColumn.description: NULL only on an erased client. Their sessions and payments stay in the trainer's book as a former client.

addColumn.name: erased_at
addColumn.description: When `erase_clients()` removed this person from this roster: either their own account was erased (every row carrying their number, on every roster), or their trainer's was (every row in that solo workspace). What stays is a nameless row for the amounts and dates to hang on until the workspace is purged. Nothing brings it back; a later invite on the same number writes a new row. `client_erased_scrubbed` makes a partial scrub unwritable. **A new personal column must be added to it in the same migration.**

alter.addCheck: erased_at IS NULL AND name IS NOT NULL OR erased_at IS NOT NULL AND deleted_at IS NOT NULL AND name IS NULL AND phone IS NULL AND goal IS NULL AND metadata IS NULL AND height_cm IS NULL AND activity_level IS NULL AND date_of_birth IS NULL AND weekly_schedule IS NULL

changeColumn.name: status
changeColumn.description: Switches a whole workspace off with one column. `closed` is how a workspace ends: there is no `deleted_at`, because `tenant` never enters sync and so needs no tombstone. Closing sets `purge_after`; the row itself is never deleted, and once purged it can never reopen (`tenant_purge`).

addColumn.name: purge_after
addColumn.description: When `purge_closed_tenants()` may hard-delete this workspace's rows. Set only on closing. Account erasure sets it to now, since nobody can reach a closed workspace and there is nothing to wait for. Workspace delete may set a grace period instead. NULL = not scheduled.

addColumn.name: purged_at
addColumn.description: When the purge ran. After it only this row is left, renamed 'Closed workspace' with `metadata` emptied at closing, because 43 foreign keys point at `tenant` from rows other workspaces keep (`trainer.home_tenant_id` among them).

alter.addCheck: (purge_after IS NULL OR status = 'closed') AND (purged_at IS NULL OR (status = 'closed' AND purge_after IS NOT NULL AND purged_at >= purge_after))

addIndex.name: idx_tenant_purge_due
addIndex.description: What the purge job asks: which closed workspaces are due.

changeColumn.name: role
changeColumn.description: The same word means the same authority in every kind of workspace. `owner` — exactly one per workspace. The row ends only through `transfer_tenant_ownership()` or `erase_account()`; after a support erasure with `leave_owned`, a workspace can have none until support assigns one. `admin` — manages people and plans; `coach` — holds a roster; `staff` — a gym's front desk or accountant, with no roster; `client` — reserved for the portal. Whether somebody coaches is whether they hold clients, not which role they have: an owner or admin may coach too. Which roles each kind of workspace allows is `tenant_role`.

changeColumn.name: deleted_at
changeColumn.description: Set only by erasure and by an ownership transfer, together with `removed`: the rows leave the partial unique indexes, so the workspace can take a new owner and the erased person is counted nowhere. An ordinary leave keeps the row live, so a rejoin can reuse it.

createTable.name: erasure_log
createTable.description: The audit that survives an erasure, holding no personal data by construction: it names ids, which point at tombstones, and counts rows. One `account` row per `erase_account()` call and one `workspace` row per workspace that call closed, completed by the purge. Not policied, and the request role holds no grants on it: it is written only by the definer functions and read by support.

column.name: kind
column.description: `account` — a person was erased. `workspace` — a workspace was closed for purging.

column.name: parent_id
column.description: On a `workspace` row, the account erasure that closed it. NULL for a workspace deleted on its own.

column.name: app_user_id
column.description: On an `account` row, the erased person: a tombstone id, no longer a person.

column.name: tenant_id
column.description: On a `workspace` row, the workspace.

column.name: requested_by
column.description: `self` when the request role called it (the person, from the app); `support` when an operator did.

column.name: completed_at
column.description: `account`: when the identity was scrubbed, which happens in the same transaction. `workspace`: when the purge ran. A `workspace` row with this NULL is a purge still owed, and the one number a DPDP question would ask for.

column.name: row_counts
column.description: `{table: rows deleted}` from the purge. Counts only, never content.

checks.check: (kind = 'account' AND app_user_id IS NOT NULL AND tenant_id IS NULL AND parent_id IS NULL) OR (kind = 'workspace' AND tenant_id IS NOT NULL AND app_user_id IS NULL)

index.name: idx_erasure_log_pending
index.description: The purge's write-back, and support's "what is still owed".

function.name: erase_account(uuid, boolean)
function.description: The only way an account ends. Called by the request role for oneself (`target = app_user_id()`); called by an operator for anyone, and only an operator may pass `leave_owned`. Refuses with `OWNS_WORKSPACE` while the person owns a live team or gym. Solo workspaces are closed and their clients erased at once; clients they coach in other workspaces stay there flagged `stale_reason = 'trainer_left'`. All their memberships end, invitations to their number are deleted, sessions are revoked, and wherever they are a client that row is erased. Last, `trainer` and `app_user` become tombstones. One transaction: an erasure is never half done. Callers cancel the UPI Autopay mandate with the provider first, since the function can only mark `subscription` cancelled.

function.name: erase_clients(uuid[])
function.description: Erases client rows, shared by both callers in `erase_account()`. Deletes everything about the person: prefs and nominee, bell, messages, feedback, milestones, assessments (the body readings), notes, reports, nudges, team activity, their plan, and bookings not yet happened. Keeps what a ledger needs, stripped of free text: logged sessions and sets, past bookings, packages, payments and receipt numbers. Not granted to anyone: reached only through `erase_account()`.

function.name: transfer_tenant_ownership(uuid, uuid)
function.description: Hands a team or gym to one of its live members: the owner, or support for a workspace left ownerless. The old owner row ends (`removed` + `deleted_at`), and their home moves if it was there. A new owner row is written, which is the only way one is ever inserted after creation (`refuse_owner_promotion()` still stops a request-role UPDATE from making one). A team also moves `team.owner_trainer_id`, so the new owner must be a trainer.

function.name: purge_tenant(uuid)
function.description: Hard-deletes every row a closed, due workspace holds, children first, and returns the counts. The one hard delete in the schema. Library rows (`exercise`, `template`, `pack`, `batch`) still used by another workspace are kept: they name no person, and deleting them would break that workspace's plans. Not granted: reached only through the job.

function.name: purge_closed_tenants(integer)
function.description: The job, run on a schedule by the backend. Purges up to `batch_size` due workspaces, oldest first, `SKIP LOCKED` so two instances never race, and completes their `erasure_log` rows.

policies.policy: Not policied, and no grants to the request role at all: only the definer functions write it, and it is read over an operator connection. Joins the not-policied list in `SCHEMA.md` with that reason.

`erase_account`, `transfer_tenant_ownership` and `purge_closed_tenants` are `REVOKE`d from PUBLIC and `GRANT EXECUTE`d to `inclineyou_app`. `erase_clients` and `purge_tenant` are revoked and granted to nobody. The request role still holds no DELETE on any table; the purge is the definer's.

code.item: `deleteAccount` stops stamping `deleted_at` and calls `erase_account(app_user_id)` after cancelling the mandate through `BillingProvider`. `OWNS_WORKSPACE` maps to a new 409 whose body names the workspaces to hand on.

`DELETE /v1/trainers/me` is rewritten: an erasure, not a soft delete; **the number IS released**, which reverses V36's rule; `OWNS_WORKSPACE` joins the error catalogue. New: `POST /v1/tenants/{id}/transfer` `{toAppUserId}` → `transfer_tenant_ownership()`. The client portal's own account delete (next release) calls the same function. `DELETE /v1/me` stays what it is: leaving one trainer, not an erasure.

The confirmation screen lists what goes (everything with a name on it), what stays (nameless amounts in workspaces they don't own), and any team or gym they must hand on first. It offers an export before the button, because the solo money book the trainer may need for their own taxes is deleted.
`phone` / `name` become nullable. Every read that shows a name draws a NULL one as "Former coach" / "Former client". Money totals must not drop an erased client's payments.
A `@Scheduled` call to `purge_closed_tenants()`, hourly. A workspace row in `erasure_log` older than a day with `completed_at` NULL raises an alert.

Our own tax invoices to the trainer are a statutory record we keep (CGST s.36). A B2C invoice below ₹50,000 need not name the recipient, so at ₹499 it names nobody. It carries a name only where the trainer gave a GSTIN, because the law requires that; confirm with the CA. The Razorpay customer is deleted through the provider's API.

New walls: the request role cannot erase anyone but itself or pass `leave_owned`; `OWNS_WORKSPACE` is raised for an owned team; a transfer to a non-member is refused; after erasure the phone signs up fresh; both scrub CHECKs refuse a partial scrub; a purge leaves an `exercise` still used by another workspace; `purge_tenant` refuses an open workspace.

proposal.title: Foreign clients: every phone in E.164, one currency per workspace, and the trainer's clock
proposal.summary: Decided 24 Sep 2026, so InclineYou can take trainers and clients outside India. The agreed tables already carry it (see `proposed-schema.html`): `tenant` gained `country`, `currency` and `timezone`; every phone column there became E.164 (`varchar(16)`, `+` and 7–15 digits, a `+91` number still a ten-digit Indian mobile); `pack` and `package` carry `(tenant_id, currency)` as a foreign key to `tenant (id, currency)`, so a workspace's money is in one currency by construction; `client.timezone` shows an online client abroad their own clock while every date and wall-clock time stays in the trainer's timezone; and `subscription` is priced by billing region from the new `plan_price` table — India ₹499 GST inclusive, Europe (the UK and Switzerland included), Asia (the Gulf included) and the rest of the world, borderline countries by the UN geoscheme. This proposal carries the same rules to the tables still under review: the rest of the money book gets the currency key, the two remaining phone columns go to E.164, the bill-number year stops assuming April–March, and a foreign client can pay by bank transfer or the trainer's payment link. Only currencies with at most two decimal places are offered, so `numeric(10,2)` stays.

changeColumn.name: currency
changeColumn.description: The workspace's currency and no other: `(tenant_id, currency)` is a foreign key to `tenant (id, currency)`, so no sum over this table adds two currencies. No default of its own — `stamp_tenant_id()` fills it from `tenant.currency` when the insert leaves it NULL. A payment is therefore always in its package's currency too.

changeColumn.name: method
changeColumn.description: How the money moved. No default any more: `upi_intent` was right for every row only while every trainer was in India. `upi_intent` is offered only in a workspace whose `tenant.country` is `IN`; `payment_link` is the trainer's `trainer_business.payment_link`; `bank_transfer` is the rail most clients abroad actually use. Validated in code.

changeColumn.name: upi_reference
changeColumn.description: The rail's own reference for the payment, whichever rail it was — the UPI UTR, a bank transfer's reference, a payment link's id. Named for the first rail and kept under that name, because the wire field is `upiReference` and old builds read it.

changeColumn.name: gym_share_amount
changeColumn.description: The gym's cut, applied at record time and stored on the row — in the payment's own `currency`.

changeColumn.name: invoice_no
changeColumn.description: `INV-<year>-<NNNN>` — the trainer's bill number, minted on request (`POST /v1/payments/{id}/invoice`), never on write, so NULL is the common case. Per trainer per numbering year, which is April–March in India and January–December elsewhere (`invoice_counter.year_start_month`), so the label is `2627` in India and `2026` abroad. Not a tax invoice and unrelated to `receipt_no`.

addColumn.name: currency
addColumn.description: The workspace's currency and no other: `(tenant_id, currency)` is a foreign key to `tenant (id, currency)`, so no sum over this table adds two currencies. No default of its own — `stamp_tenant_id()` fills it from `tenant.currency` when the insert leaves it NULL.

changeColumn.name: period
changeColumn.description: `'YYYY-MM'`, a calendar month in the trainer's timezone. A month is the unit gyms settle on, in India and elsewhere.

changeColumn.name: fy
changeColumn.description: The calendar year the numbering year starts in — `2026` for April 2026 – March 2027 in India, and for January–December 2026 elsewhere. One encoding for both, so the column never has to be read against the country; the label on the bill is derived (`2627` when `year_start_month = 4`, `2026` when it is 1).

addColumn.name: year_start_month
addColumn.description: Which month this numbering year began in: 4 (April) when the trainer's solo workspace is in India, 1 (January) everywhere else. Frozen on the row, so a bill's number can always be re-read. A trainer who changes country keeps the running year to its end and starts the other kind at the next boundary — never mid-year, which is the one way two rows could claim the same bill.

addColumn.name: currency
addColumn.description: The currency of `amount`, set together with it (`client_notification_amount_currency`), so "paid 2,000" can say of what. The workspace's currency, by the same `(tenant_id, currency)` key as the money book.

addColumn.name: currency
addColumn.description: The currency of `amount`, set together with it (`trainer_notification_amount_currency`). The workspace's currency, by the same `(tenant_id, currency)` key as the money book.

changeColumn.name: invited_phone
changeColumn.description: Kept after binding rather than cleared — it is the evidence of who was invited, and a person's number can change afterwards. E.164, like `app_user.phone`.

alter.addCheck: invited_phone IS NULL OR (invited_phone ~ '^\+[1-9][0-9]{6,14}$' AND (invited_phone !~ '^\+91' OR invited_phone ~ '^\+91[6-9][0-9]{9}$'))

changeColumn.name: nominee_phone
changeColumn.description: The nominee's number, in E.164 like every phone column — a client abroad may well name somebody at home. Removed with the row when the client leaves; never contacted.

alter.addCheck: nominee_phone IS NULL OR (nominee_phone ~ '^\+[1-9][0-9]{6,14}$' AND (nominee_phone !~ '^\+91' OR nominee_phone ~ '^\+91[6-9][0-9]{9}$'))

changeColumn.name: gstin
changeColumn.description: The gym's GST number. Asked only when the workspace's `tenant.country` is `IN`, and NULL elsewhere: GST is India's, and a gym abroad invoices under its own regime, which gets a column when a gym there needs one.

addColumn.name: timezone
addColumn.description: The branch's IANA zone when it differs from the gym's `tenant.timezone` — one chain across Dubai and London. NULL = the gym's. Validated with `ZoneId.of` in code.

changeColumn.name: week_start
changeColumn.description: Monday, everywhere — the ISO week, as the day strip draws it. A `DATE`, because a week is a week in the trainer's timezone and not an instant.

code.item: Hardcode India: `wa.me/91${digits}`, a `+91 ` display prefix, and a match on the last ten digits. With E.164 stored, a `wa.me` link is the digits after `+`, display is libphonenumber's, and matching is equality.

item.where: web lib · money, packs, clients, nudges, portal

code.item: `₹` and `en-IN` are written into about a dozen formatters. Money is formatted from the row's `currency` with `Intl.NumberFormat`; `en-IN` grouping (lakh, crore) stays for INR.
Every phone `@Pattern` becomes one E.164 validator (libphonenumber), with the default region read from the active workspace's `tenant.country`.
Country → `india` · `europe` · `asia` · `rest_of_world`: the Gulf is asia, the UK and Switzerland europe, everything else by the UN geoscheme (M49).

Asks the country (prefilled from the number's calling code) and writes `tenant.country`, `currency` and `timezone`, `trainer.timezone` and `subscription.billing_country` / `price_region` before any price exists.

review.summary: A whole-schema review on 24 Sep 2026 against the v1 scope (the trainer web app alone) and the three releases after it. Every finding below was checked against the live catalogue and the code that writes each table, not against the documentation. Those marked `fixed · V21` are closed by `V21__schema_review_hardening.sql` and the three small code changes that shipped with it (`TenantContext.SYSTEM` for the exercise seeder, `OtpRequestSweeper`, the new `subscription` table's trigger). The rest are application code or product decisions that a migration cannot make, and are listed so they are not lost.

finding.title: Any request could write the global exercise library
finding.detail: The tier-3 policy on `exercise` was one clause for every command with no actor test, so its WITH CHECK admitted any row whose `tenant_id` is NULL. A client session, a bootstrap session or a connection with no context at all could add to, edit or tombstone the library every trainer builds from, and a custom movement written with `is_custom = false` skipped the stamp trigger and went global. The only thing writing global rows legitimately — `ExerciseSeeder` — did so through the request role with an empty context, which is why nothing noticed.
finding.fix: Split into a read policy (unchanged), a staff write policy for custom rows in the active workspace only, and a seed policy for global rows that only the new `system` actor satisfies. `ExerciseSeeder` declares `TenantContext.SYSTEM` around its upsert; no request context can be it.

finding.title: The request role could hard-delete from every table, and every future table was born writable
finding.detail: `inclineyou_app` held SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE on all 46 tables, although nothing in the product is hard-deleted except `attention_dismissal` and swept `web_session` rows. It could also UPDATE the three append-only logs (`package_adjustment`, `client_assignment`, `team_activity`). And `ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES` granted all four on every table created later, so a new table was fully writable by requests before anybody had written its policy.
finding.fix: DELETE revoked everywhere except `attention_dismissal`, `web_session` and `otp_request` (which now has a sweeper); UPDATE revoked on the three logs; the default privilege revoked, so a migration that creates a table grants what it needs beside its policies.

finding.title: `portal_change_client_phone()` moved any number to any number when the caller had no phone set
finding.detail: V20 read an empty `app_phone()` as "no session phone, so skip the check". Any request-role connection without a phone — a scheduler, a boot runner, a bug — could therefore move every roster row and the identity row from one number to another. It never checked the caller was a client either.
finding.fix: Under the request role it now requires `app_actor() = 'client'` and `app_phone() = old_phone`, with no empty-string escape. The owner (tests, a DBA) keeps V20's behaviour, told apart by `session_user`, which a SECURITY DEFINER function does not change.

finding.title: `mint_trainer_notification()` wrote into any trainer's bell
finding.detail: It accepted any recipient and any client. Today's two callers check ownership first, but the database did not, so one wrong id put a stranger's client name and an amount into another trainer's notifications.
finding.fix: The recipient must be a live member of the client's workspace — true for the coach, a team owner, and a coach a client was reassigned away from. A refused mint returns NULL rather than failing the write that caused it (the V18 rule).

finding.title: Any workspace member could rename the workspace, and any staff request could mint an owner
finding.detail: `tenant_self` was FOR ALL with no actor or role test, so a coach — or a client whose read scope included the workspace — could UPDATE its name, status or `primary_app_user_id`. `tenant_member_tenant` was FOR ALL too, so a staff request could INSERT a membership with `role = 'owner'`. No request code writes either table that way; only the definer triggers do.
finding.fix: `tenant`: SELECT for members, UPDATE for its owner, no INSERT. `tenant_member`: SELECT and UPDATE only, plus `refuse_owner_promotion()`, which refuses a request-role UPDATE that makes somebody an owner.

finding.title: A child row could sit in a different workspace from its parent
finding.detail: `stamp_tenant_id()` takes the active workspace before it looks at the parent row, and nothing compared the two. A payment against a pack in workspace A, written while standing in B, was stamped B — and because tier 2 reads one workspace at a time, each side looked complete. Impossible in v1 (one workspace per trainer); silent when workspaces ship.
finding.fix: `UNIQUE (id, tenant_id)` on `client`, `package`, `program` and `workout_session`, and fourteen composite foreign keys on `(parent_id, tenant_id)` across twelve child tables, validated against the data.

finding.title: `app_owns_tenant()` was executable by PUBLIC
finding.detail: PUBLIC execute made it a yes/no oracle over other people's workspaces for any role that can connect. It looks like it should be STABLE and must stay VOLATILE: creating a team inserts the tenant row in a BEFORE trigger of the same statement, and a STABLE function reads the statement's starting snapshot and cannot see it. Making it STABLE broke team creation in `TenantIsolationTest` while V21 was being written.
finding.fix: EXECUTE revoked from PUBLIC and granted to the request role; VOLATILE kept, with the reason written into V21.

finding.title: `otp_request` was never purged
finding.detail: V1 promised a scheduled cleanup that was never written (`SessionSweeper` says so). Every sign-in since the first has left a phone number behind — personal data kept past its purpose.
finding.fix: `OtpRequestSweeper`, hourly, removes rows older than `app.otp.purge-after-days` (30) whose lock has run out; the send ceiling reads one day and the lock ten minutes, so nothing live is touched.

finding.title: Closing an account does not end its sessions — the deleted account keeps working
finding.detail: `AccountService.close` sets `deleted_at` on `trainer` and `app_user` and revokes nothing. `TenantScope.resolve` falls back to `homeTenantOf(trainerId)`, which has no `deleted_at` filter, so a live 7-day JWT or 72-hour session still gets a full staff context. A phone change is the same: other sessions survive it.
finding.fix: Revoke every session for the subject on close and on phone change, and make `homeTenantOf` and `AuthTokenFilter` refuse a deleted trainer. JWTs need a per-trainer `tokens_valid_after` — the IDENTITY.md key-rotation work.

finding.title: Nothing refuses to boot on the development JWT secret
finding.detail: `app.jwt.secret` defaults to a value published in the repository, and the same key signs every token kind, including the 10-minute phone-change ticket, which is also accepted as a bearer token on several authenticated routes.
finding.fix: Fail boot when `JWT_SECRET` is the default outside the `dev` profile; give tickets their own audience claim and refuse them as bearer tokens.

finding.title: The three-attempt OTP cap can be raced
finding.detail: `OtpService.verify` checks the lock, then compares with bcrypt (about 100 ms), and only then records the wrong attempt. Concurrent guesses all pass the lock check first, so far more than three guesses per code are evaluated, bounded only by the 300-per-minute auth tier.
finding.fix: Increment the attempt counter atomically before comparing (Redis INCR, or an `UPDATE … RETURNING` on `otp_request`), and refuse once it passes the cap.

finding.title: The web never sends `X-InclineYou-Client: web`
finding.detail: So the browser holds an irrevocable 7-day JWT and `web_session` is never written. The whole revocable-session design (V41) is unused by the one client v1 ships.
finding.fix: Send the header from the web's server-side fetch; then S9's revocation actually reaches a browser.

finding.title: A session cookie is accepted while CSRF protection is off
finding.detail: `AuthTokenFilter` reads the `inclineyou_session` cookie, CSRF is disabled, and the backend sets no SameSite policy of its own. Whether that is exploitable depends entirely on how the web sets the cookie.
finding.fix: Either stop accepting the cookie at the API (the web proxies with a header), or require SameSite=Lax at minimum and an Origin check on state-changing requests.

finding.title: The database identity check warns rather than fails, and the owner role is a superuser locally
finding.detail: `DatabaseIdentityCheck` logs a warning when RLS is inert and runs after `ExerciseSeeder` has written. Locally the owner `inclineyou` is a superuser with BYPASSRLS, so every SECURITY DEFINER function runs as superuser. FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is deliberately not applied: the definer functions rely on the owner bypassing the policies.
finding.fix: Outside `dev`, fail boot if the pool's role is a superuser, has BYPASSRLS or owns the tables. In production the migration owner must be a plain, non-superuser role.

finding.title: Row-level security reads settings that any SQL statement can change
finding.detail: The policies read `app.actor`, `app.tenant_ids` and friends, which the request role may `set_config` itself. RLS here is a backstop against a query that forgot its `trainer_id` filter, not against SQL injection. The review found no SQL built from user input — every dynamic fragment is a code constant and every value a bound parameter.
finding.fix: None needed now. Keep the no-string-built-SQL rule; it is what makes this acceptable.

finding.title: Session settings are rewritten on borrow but never reset on return
finding.detail: `TenantAwareDataSource`'s Javadoc says the six settings are cleared when a connection goes back to the pool; nothing does that. It is safe today only because Hikari autocommits the `set_config` call — with `auto-commit=false` a rollback would restore the previous borrower's values for the rest of the borrow.
finding.fix: Reset in a `close()` wrapper, or correct the Javadoc and pin `auto-commit=true` with a comment.

finding.title: Forty-six tables, seven CHECK constraints
finding.detail: Nothing stopped a negative payment, a percentage over a hundred, a working window that ends before it starts, a malformed settlement period, or a state-machine value no code branches on — `payment.status`, `package.status`, `scheduled_session.status` among them. Profile vocabularies stay in Java by V6's decision; these are the other kind, where a value outside the set is a corrupt row rather than a new answer.
finding.fix: Status, money, range and format CHECKs, each value list taken from every writer (backend SQL, the phone's sync push, the seed scripts), added NOT VALID and then validated.

finding.title: Three synced tables took `updated_at` from the device
finding.detail: `working_hours`, `time_block` and `batch` had no `set_updated_at` trigger, and their sync upserts write `updated_at = EXCLUDED.updated_at` from the phone. A device with a wrong clock, or a replayed record, wrote a past timestamp and the edit became invisible to every other device's pull. Four more tables (`client_note`, `nudge_template`, `attention_dismissal`, `invoice_counter`) relied on each writer remembering.
finding.fix: `set_updated_at` triggers on all seven, so the server's clock always wins.

finding.title: `scheduled_session.pack_package_id` had no foreign key
finding.detail: The one column that ties the diary to the money book — which package a done session was charged to — was checked by nothing.
finding.fix: A foreign key to `package`, plus the same-workspace composite key.

finding.title: The catalogue's dead media columns could be refilled
finding.detail: `exercise.image_url` and `video_url` survived V22 in the baseline. The seeder writes NULL on purpose (the Gym visual artwork is unlicensed), but only the seeder kept that rule.
finding.fix: A CHECK that a catalogue row carries no media, and that any URL a custom row carries is http(s) — never a `javascript:` URL rendered as a link.

finding.title: The session-logging hot path read along unindexed foreign keys
finding.detail: Opening the log for a booked session (`workout_session.scheduled_session_id`), "last time" and exercise history (`workout_session` by client and date), and every amount-due figure (`payment.package_id`, summed per pack) had no index. Nor did `scheduled_session.program_id`, `workout_session.program_id`, `program.template_id`, `package.pack_id` or `workout_exercise.exercise_id`.
finding.fix: Nine indexes, partial on `deleted_at` where the reads are.

finding.title: Twenty-six indexes only cost writes
finding.detail: Each was a strict prefix of another index on the same table with the same predicate — twenty of them the `idx_<t>_tenant` twin of `idx_<t>_tenant_trainer`.
finding.fix: Dropped. The composite indexes still serve the same lookups and back the same foreign keys.

finding.title: No trial clock — MUST-16's blocker
finding.detail: No subscription table or trial timestamp existed. The trial is the one billing component that cannot be added after the first signup: a trainer recorded without a start has no honest expiry.
finding.fix: `subscription`, one row per trainer, created by trigger on trainer insert so no signup path can skip it; no `tenant_id` (a seat is a coaching trainer who spans workspaces); state machine and plan as CHECKs; provider columns ready for the rail. The Plan & trial screen and the free-tier cap are still code to write.

finding.title: Assessments cannot be completed in v1
finding.detail: `readings`, `answers` and `completed_at` are written only by the portal. With the portal off, a trainer can build, send and read an assessment that never comes back.
finding.fix: V21 adds `assessment.entered_by` (client | trainer), so a trainer-entered answer is never shown as the client's own. The trainer write route and its screen are still to build.

finding.title: A web-only trainer has no way to record a measurement
finding.detail: The web only reads `body_metric`; it never calls the POST. V14 says assessment readings are never copied into `body_metric`. So the measurement history and trends in v1 stay empty unless the phone or portal wrote them.
finding.fix: A product call: a quick-measure write on the web, or let a trainer-entered assessment (M2) feed the chart with its source labelled.

finding.title: `WeeklyReportJob` silently does nothing behind the wall
finding.detail: The Monday cron runs with no RLS context, so its `SELECT … FROM client` returns zero rows and its `nudge_log` insert would fail WITH CHECK. TENANCY.md warned about exactly this job.
finding.fix: Set a staff context per trainer inside the job — or retire it with the table, which v1 does not use.

finding.title: Three v1 surfaces read tables nothing in v1 writes
finding.detail: `trainer_notification` is minted only by the portal and by team reassignment, so the v1 bell is empty. `client_message` has no writer anywhere. `exercise.level`, `secondary_targets` and `form_cues` are rendered but never filled.
finding.fix: No schema change. Worth deciding whether the bell ships in v1 at all.

finding.title: No time zone anywhere
finding.detail: `workout_session.session_date` is a DATE and working hours are minutes past midnight, both in a zone nobody wrote down. The first trainer coaching a Gulf client online is the first wrong date.
finding.fix: `trainer.timezone`, an IANA name defaulting to Asia/Kolkata — what every row so far assumed.

finding.title: Phone numbers are bare ten-digit Indian numbers
finding.detail: Every product path stores a ten-digit Indian national number with no country code, but nothing in the database says so: the sync push stores `client.phone` as sent, `team_member.invited_phone` keeps whatever the web form held (spaces, `+91`), and the test fixtures and seeds write nine- and twelve-digit numbers. A format CHECK today would break the suite and the sync push.
finding.fix: One normaliser on every write path first (the two `normalizePhone` helpers only build `wa.me` links and never store), then a CHECK. Moving to E.164 (`+91…`) is the same migration, best done before the phone app ships.

finding.title: One push token per trainer
finding.detail: `trainer.fcm_token` holds one device, so a second phone or web push overwrites the first.
finding.fix: A `device` table when the phone app ships. Not v1.

finding.title: Nothing is ever erased
finding.detail: Soft delete is forever. Closing an account keeps the trainer's phone, name and email and every client's name, phone, notes, measurements and payments; removing a client keeps the same. The DPDP Act expects erasure once consent is withdrawn or the purpose is served.
finding.fix: An erasure pass after a retention window: anonymise names, phones and free text in place (the rows and money totals must survive for sync and the books), run by the owner role on a schedule. Needs a product and legal decision on the window.

finding.title: Health answers live in `assessment` JSON
finding.detail: Vitals, visceral fat and "did anything hurt" are stored in `readings` / `answers`, by the product owner's decision. Blood pressure and resting heart rate are hidden in v1, but the catalogue still has them.
finding.fix: Keep them isolable in `AssessmentCatalogue`, as recorded. Encryption at rest is the provider's.

finding.title: Every new trainer's workspace has no owner and is named after their phone number
finding.detail: `claimTrainer` saves the `trainer` row before the `app_user` row. `ensure_home_tenant` runs on the trainer insert, finds no account, and writes `primary_app_user_id = NULL` and `name` = the phone (which is what `trainer.name` holds at that point). `ensure_membership_for_user` later adds the owner membership but nothing fills `primary_app_user_id`, so `app_owns_tenant()` answers no and `tenant_owner_update` refuses the owner a rename of their own workspace. The name never follows the trainer's either.
finding.fix: Ownership moves to the owner membership, which the two triggers already write whichever row lands second; the phone-as-name is treated as no name, and a solo workspace follows its trainer's name until renamed.

finding.title: The owner is recorded three times and nothing keeps the copies equal
finding.detail: `tenant.primary_app_user_id`, `tenant_member.role = 'owner'` and `team.owner_trainer_id`. The ownership test reads the first, the promotion guard the second, and nothing limits a workspace to one live owner. T1 is these copies drifting apart.
finding.fix: `primary_app_user_id` dropped; `uq_tenant_member_owner` makes the owner row exactly one; `team.owner_trainer_id` stays only until `team_member` folds into `tenant_member`.

finding.title: A workspace's kind can be changed
finding.detail: Nothing freezes `tenant.type`, so a solo workspace could become a gym and take every row in it along.
finding.fix: `freeze_tenant_type()`, and the composite keys on `(id, type)` would refuse it anyway once anything points at them.

finding.title: Two teams could share one workspace
finding.detail: No unique index on `team.tenant_id`.
finding.fix: `uq_team_tenant`.

finding.title: The gym is planned twice
finding.detail: The schema already has `tenant.type = 'gym'` and `gym_admin` / `gym_staff` roles, while the gym PRD plans a standalone `gym` table with its own `owner_app_user_id` and a `gym_staff` table with a different role list. Building the PRD would add another owner record and put staff in two tables.
finding.fix: `tenant` is the parent of every kind; `gym` is a one-to-one table keyed by `tenant_id`, `gym_branch` hangs off it, and staff are `tenant_member` rows.

finding.title: Roles are one flat list with no rule for which kind of workspace allows which
finding.detail: `owner, admin, coach, gym_admin, gym_staff, client` mixes team words and gym words, nothing stops `gym_staff` in a solo workspace, and every new role (the PRD's `front_desk`) is a CHECK rewrite on a live table.
finding.fix: Workspace-neutral roles (`owner · admin · coach · staff · client`) and a `tenant_role (tenant_type, role)` lookup enforced by composite foreign keys.

finding.title: There is nowhere to invite somebody who has no account
finding.detail: `tenant_member.status` allows `invited`, but `app_user_id` is NOT NULL, so it can only invite people who already signed up. `team_member` keeps `invited_phone` for this, and the gym PRD would have kept a third copy on `gym_staff`.
finding.fix: `tenant_invite`, claimed through `respond_tenant_invite()`; `tenant_member.status` narrows to `active · removed`.

finding.title: A membership has no history
finding.detail: No `invited_by`, `joined_at` or `ended_at`. Who added a gym's front-desk account, and when they left, is an audit question.
finding.fix: The three columns, with a CHECK tying `ended_at` to `removed`.

finding.title: Editing a coach's share rewrites past revenue
finding.detail: The two percentages are edited in place and `TenantRevenueService` applies the current value to every payment, so 60% → 70% changes last quarter's figures.
finding.fix: `tenant_member_terms`, dated and append-only; revenue uses the terms in force on each payment's date.

finding.title: Loose ends on `tenant`
finding.detail: `metadata` holds only back-pointers that other columns already hold; `deleted_at` is a second way to end a workspace beside `status = 'closed'` on a table that never syncs; `idx_tenant_type` indexes three values nothing filters on.
finding.fix: `metadata` gets the rule that nothing branches on it; `deleted_at` and `idx_tenant_type` dropped; `status_changed_at` added.
